Using a Jenkins image as a base for installing WSO2 Identity Server is generally not recommended for several reasons. While Jenkins images do come with some development tools pre-installed, they are primarily designed for CI/CD processes and not for serving as application servers like WSO2 Identity Server.

### Recommended Approach

1. **Use a Minimal Ubuntu/Debian Image:**
   Since your worst-case scenario is starting with a bare Ubuntu image, a minimal Ubuntu or Debian image is a solid option. This allows you to control which packages are installed and keep the installation lightweight.

   Here's a simple Dockerfile to get you started with WSO2 Identity Server on an Ubuntu base:

   ```Dockerfile
   FROM ubuntu:20.04

   # Install dependencies
   RUN apt-get update && \
       apt-get install -y openjdk-8-jdk maven ant wget && \
       apt-get clean && \
       rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

   # Set JAVA_HOME
   ENV JAVA_HOME /usr/lib/jvm/java-8-openjdk-amd64
   ENV PATH $PATH:$JAVA_HOME/bin

   # Download and install WSO2 Identity Server
   RUN wget https://product-dist.wso2.com/wso2/identity-server/5.10.0/wso2is-5.10.0.zip && \
       unzip wso2is-5.10.0.zip -d /opt && \
       rm wso2is-5.10.0.zip

   # Expose ports
   EXPOSE 9443 9763

   # Define entrypoint
   WORKDIR /opt/wso2is-5.10.0/bin
   CMD ["sh", "wso2server.sh"]
   ```

   Replace `5.10.0` with the desired version of WSO2 Identity Server.

2. **Using Docker Compose:**
   If your application has dependencies on other services (like databases), consider using Docker Compose for easier orchestration.

3. **Use Official WSO2 Docker Images:**
   WSO2 provides official Docker images for its Identity Server. You can leverage these images as a starting point, which will save you a lot of configuration overhead. The official images are available on Docker Hub. Here’s how you can use a WSO2 Identity Server Docker image:

   ```yaml
   version: '3'
   services:
     wso2is:
       image: wso2/wso2-identity-server:5.11.0
       ports:
         - "9443:9443"
         - "9763:9763"
       environment:
         - JAVA_OPTS=-Duser.timezone=UTC
   ```

### Conclusion

Using a Jenkins image as a base is not ideal for running WSO2 Identity Server, as it introduces unnecessary dependencies and complexity. Instead, opt for a minimal base image or use the official WSO2 Docker images, which already come preconfigured and ready for deployment. This approach minimizes setup time and potential issues arising from unnecessary components.

title: Unity3D: Resource.Load defined AudioClip ends up Null going into the AudioSource
ground_truth_answer:
First a general note: Never use + "/" for system file paths! Rather sue Path.Combine which automatically inserts the correct path separators according to the platform it is running on

string file in System.IO.Directory.GetFiles(Path.Combine(Application.dataPath, "Resources", "Audio", "BGM"))

Then please read the documentation of Resources.Load!

  1. It requires your file(s) being placed inside a folder called Resources which is compiled into the application build and therefore can not be changed afterwards. This seems to be the case for you.

  2. It does not take a full system path like you pass in since Directory.GetFiles returns

    An array of the full names (including paths) for the files in the specified directory

    but rather expects a path within all Resources folders - yes you can have multiple ones.

    Let's say e.g. you put your files in a structure like

    Assets
|--Resources
|  |--someFile.mp3
|
|--SomeOtherFolder
|  |--Resources
|  |  |--someOtherFile.mp3
|  |  |--ASubFolder
|  |  |  |--yetAnotherFile.mp3

    Then you would address these by using

    Resources.Load<AudioClip>("someFile");
Resources.Load<AudioClip>("someOtherFile");
Resources.Load<AudioClip>("ASubfolder/yetAnotherFile");

    since when build all Resources are packed together.

    So in your case it should be

    Resources.Load<AudioClip>("Audio/BGM/" + formatted1);

    where you have to make sure that formatted1 is not a full path but only the filename! You can simply use Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension so you don't even need your replace

    var formatted1 = Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(file);

  3. It is bad ^^

    In their Best Practices for the Resources folder Unity themselves recommend

    Don't use it!

However

Since it is not recommneded to use the Resources at all I would rather recommend:

If you don't want to change them later

You can't change the Resources afterwards for e.g. replacing a file. So if you can't change the files later anyway, then why not rather directly reference them in the places where they are needed later?

Simply put your audio files in a folder that is not Resources and reference them in your scripts directly where you need them:

// Simply drag&drop the clip into this field via the Inspector in Unity
[SerializeField] private AudioClip someClip;

If you want to change them later

In case you actually would like to be able to replace them later also after a build you could instead use UnityWebRequestMultimedia.GetAudioClip which can also be used to load files from a system file on runtime. For this you wouldn't put your files into the Resources or any other folder but rather either the StreamingAssets or the Application.persistentDataPath.

I usually go:

  • In the editor use StreamingAssets folder so all stuff lies inside the project and access it via Application.streamingAssetsPath
  • In a build first check if file exists in Application.persistentDataPath
  • If not copy it from Application.streamingAssetsPath and store it into Application.persistentDataPath
  • otherwise simply load it from Application.persistentDataPath

Modified API Example

[RequireComponent(typeof(AudioSource))]
public class AudioExample : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private AudioSource _audioSource;

    public List<AudioClip> LoadedAudioClips = new List<AudioClip>;

    private List<UnityWebRequest> _runningWebRequests = new List<UnityWebRequest>();

    private void Awake()
    {
        if(!_audioSource) _audioSource = GetComponent<AudioSource>();
    }

    private void Start()
    {
        StartCoroutine(GetAudioClip());
    }

    private IEnumerator GetAudioClip()
    {
        foreach(string file in System.IO.Directory.GetFiles(Path.Combine(Application.persistentDataPath, "Audio", "BGM"))
        {
            if(!file.EndsWith(System.IO.Patch.GetExtension(".mp3"))) continue;

            UnityWebRequest www = UnityWebRequestMultimedia.GetAudioClip("file:///" + file, AudioType.MPEG);
            {
               _runningWebRequests.Add(www);
               www.Send();
            }
        }

        while(_runningWebRequests.Count > 0)
        {
            foreach(var www in _runningWebRequests.Where(www => www.isDone))
            {
                _runningWebRequests.Remove(www);

                if (www.isError)
                {
                    Debug.LogWarning(www.error);
                }
                else
                {
                    var clip = DownloadHandlerAudioClip.GetContent(www);
                    if(clip == null)
                    {
                        Debug.LogError("Huh?!");
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        LoadedAudioClips.Add(clip);
                    }
                }
            }

            yield return null;
        }
    }
}

Also saw you comments so:

StreamingAssets is also a special folder you can store files in you want to read in on runtime. It is local. Also this folder is not "visible" from the outside and can not be altered later.

If you need to be able to alter stuff later (like e.g. also saving files) you will always need to use the Application.persistentDataPath instead.

HTML5 has double standards, in the sense that it prohibits authors/document from using some constructs and yet requires or recommends browsers (and other user agents) to support them. So if you use frameborder, your document is non-conforming. Yet it is “expected” to be supported in a specific way.

The situation is in principle similar with the scrolling attribute. Its expected effect is that values on, scroll, and yes cause scrolling bars (like overflow: scroll), values off, noscroll, and no prevent scroll bars; and value auto causes scrollbars when content does not fit (the default). However, none of Firefox, Chrome, IE seems to support the values that cause scrolling bars unconditionally, and only Firefox supports all of the values that prevent them, whereas Chrome and IE support just no.

This is understandable in the sense that scrolling=no is the attribute that browsers have traditionally supported. The other values are more or less an invention in the HTML5 draft, probably supposed to cover some values actually in use or supported.

The bottom line with this is that scrolling=no works. To cause scrollbars even when not needed for the content, scrolling=yes is not useful in practice (the corresponding CSS setting works).

To address the issue of unwanted scrollbars in your Facebook app, here are a few considerations and potential solutions:

### 1. Verify Auto-Resize Configuration
Ensure that your app is configured to resize automatically. If it's not set up correctly, even the defined width may not render properly within the Facebook iframe, leading to scrollbars. You can check the app settings in the Facebook developer portal to confirm that "Auto-Resize" is enabled.

### 2. Box-Sizing Property
Facebook apps loaded within iframes might not consistently support CSS3 properties, including the `box-sizing` property. While many modern browsers support it, Facebook's iframe context can have its restrictions. Ensure you're using the correct version:

```css
* {
    box-sizing: border-box; /* Use this for all elements */
}
```

If there are issues with the property being applied, consider using `padding` without `box-sizing` as a fallback:

```css
.container {
    width: 500px; 
    padding: 10px; /* Adjust as needed */
    margin: 0; /* Avoid margin, which can contribute to overflow */
}
```

### 3. Width Calculations
If you're defining a width of 500px and adding padding, the total rendered width could exceed the specified width, contributing to the scrollbars. If you're setting `padding` of 10px on both sides (20px total), ensure that the actual width of your content does not exceed `500px`, or adjust accordingly:

```css
.container {
    width: calc(500px - 20px); /* Subtract total padding */
    padding: 10px;
}
```

### 4. Inspect the Iframe's Content
Sometimes, content such as images or fixed-width elements inside your app can cause overflow and trigger scrollbars. Inspect the elements to ensure they fit within your defined width, or set them to have a max-width of 100%:

```css
img {
    max-width: 100%;
    height: auto; /* Keep aspect ratio */
}
```

### 5. Using CSS Overflow Properties
If all else fails, you can control scroll behavior using the `overflow` property:

```css
.container {
    overflow: hidden; /* Prevent scrollbars, but ensure this doesn't cut off important content */
}
```

### Summary
1. Confirm Auto-Resize is enabled in your app settings.
2. Ensure consistent use of the `box-sizing` property across all elements.
3. Adjust your width calculations considering padding.
4. Inspect and adjust inner content to avoid overflow.
5. Consider using CSS properties to manage scrolling behavior.

Testing these adjustments should help eliminate the unwanted scrollbars in your Facebook app. For the box-sizing support, it's best to test on different browsers and devices to ensure compatibility within the Facebook iframe environment.

The error message you’re encountering (`standard_init_linux.go:219: exec user process caused: exec format error`) typically indicates that the architecture of the Docker image you are trying to run does not match the architecture of the Raspberry Pi, which uses an ARM architecture (typically ARMv7 or ARM64).

Here's a step-by-step guide to resolving this issue:

### 1. Use an ARM-Compatible Jenkins Image

First, ensure that you are using an ARM-compatible Jenkins Docker image. The default Jenkins image may be built for amd64, which is incompatible with Raspberry Pi's architecture. You can use the following ARM-compatible image instead:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jenkins
  namespace: jenkins
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jenkins
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: jenkins
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: jenkins
        image: arm64v8/jenkins:latest  # Use this ARM-compatible image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        - containerPort: 50000
        volumeMounts:
        - name: jenkins-home
          mountPath: /var/jenkins_home
      volumes:
      - name: jenkins-home
        emptyDir: {}
```

### 2. Create the Namespace

Before deploying Jenkins, make sure you have created the namespace:

```bash
kubectl create namespace jenkins
```

### 3. Apply the Deployment

Once you have updated your `jenkins-deployment.yaml` file with the ARM-compatible image, apply the file again:

```bash
kubectl apply -f jenkins-deployment.yaml -n jenkins
```

### 4. Expose the Jenkins Service

You also need to expose the Jenkins service. You can do that by creating a `NodePort` service definition, which could look something like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: jenkins-service
  namespace: jenkins
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
    nodePort: 30000  # or any other free port
  selector:
    app: jenkins
```

Deploy it:

```bash
kubectl apply -f jenkins-service.yaml -n jenkins
```

### 5. Accessing Jenkins

After deploying, you can access Jenkins by navigating to `http://<raspberry-pi-ip>:30000` in your web browser. The default admin password can be found in the logs like this:

```bash
kubectl logs <jenkins-pod-name> -n jenkins
```

Replace `<jenkins-pod-name>` with the name of your Jenkins pod, and look for the password in the startup logs.

### 6. Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues, check the logs of the Jenkins pod using:

```bash
kubectl logs <jenkins-pod-name> -n jenkins
```

Make sure that your microk8s is running properly and that you have sufficient resources allocated for Jenkins, as it may require more memory and CPU, especially when running builds.

By following the steps outlined above, you should be able to deploy Jenkins on your microk8s cluster running on Raspberry Pi successfully.

The WCF framework is part of .NET 3.0 and not .NET 3.5, so you don't need .NET 3.5 in the clients.

Also with WCF you can provide services that are based on the web services standards. These services can be used even with the "old" web service clients, or other platforms, like Java.

The credential based WCF message security is fulfilling the WS-Security 1.1 standard, which can also be used with a WSE client.

http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms735093.aspx: WCF supports a wide variety of interoperability scenarios. The BasicHttpBinding class is targeted at the Basic Security Profile (BSP) and the WSHttpBinding class is targeted at the latest security standards, such as WS-Security 1.1 and WS-SecureConversation. By adhering to these standards, WCF security can interoperate and integrate with Web services that are hosted on operating systems and platforms other than Microsoft Windows.

I would definitely go for the WCF solution and not the WSE. I see WCF as a direct successor of WSE, which is not imporved further by Microsoft (even the WSE home link is broken from the WSE 3.0 download page).

As Alex mentioned, connecting to non-MS platform, despite the standards, might be challenging. A proof of concept is definitely neccessary in these scenarios.

Q: What are the benefits of migrating our application over to WCF as opposed to continuing to use .NET Remoting? A:

There are plenty of reasons to ditch remoting; a few might include:

  • lack of transport flexibility
  • versioning requirements are huge pain
  • platform dependent (no sensible chance of cross-platform usage)
  • no chance of usage from the growing mobile market
  • lack of future development: whatever feature you want added - it won't be

however, I would disagree that WCF is the automatic replacement; WCF itself is a pretty versatile tool, but can be pretty complex, and has restrictions of its own. I haven't used it myself, but I have seen lots of praise for Service Stack, essentially with users describing it as "WCF done right", i.e. the good bits of WCF, without the pain points. However, there are plenty of other options too. One nice thing about the idea of Service Stack, though, is that it iterates pretty quickly, and if it lacks something you want you can change it.

To decide on the best approach for securing your web service with .NET 3.5 while accommodating clients using .NET 3.0, we need to consider the capabilities and limitations of both WCF and WSE 3.0. Here’s how you can approach the situation:

### Understanding WCF and WSE 3.0

1. **WCF (Windows Communication Foundation)**:
   - WCF is a robust framework introduced in .NET 3.0 for building service-oriented applications. It supports various protocols and bindings and provides security features out of the box.
   - If you choose to implement WCF in .NET 3.5, you can take advantage of enhanced features and better security mechanisms (such as message encryption, transport security, and security through standards like WS-Security).
   - However, WCF services created in .NET 3.5 can still be consumed by .NET 3.0 clients, but there may be limitations and issues specific to the binding and configuration used.

2. **WSE 3.0 (Web Services Enhancements)**:
   - WSE is an older technology designed to add advanced capabilities to ASMX web services (like security features). As of now, WSE is considered deprecated in favor of WCF.
   - While it can help you secure your old ASMX services, implementing security features with WSE might lead to complexities and issues, especially since it has known compatibility issues with Visual Studio 2008 and post-.NET 3.0 platforms.

### Recommendations

#### Option 1: Use WCF with .NET 3.5
- **Developing the Service**:
  - Create your web service using WCF in .NET 3.5. This will give you access to more reliable security features.
  - Configure your WCF service to use a binding that is compatible with .NET 3.0 clients, such as `basicHttpBinding` which is SOAP 1.1 compliant and widely supported.

- **Security Configuration**:
  - Implement transport security with SSL (HTTPS) for secure communication.
  - Consider using message security if the clients can handle it, which might involve pre-shared keys or certificates.

- **Client Compatibility**:
  - .NET 3.0 clients should be capable of consuming WCF services, keeping in mind that you may need to adjust your configurations based on security features.

#### Option 2: Use WSE 3.0 with ASMX
- If you want a simpler approach and are familiar with ASMX services, you can consider using WSE 3.0.
- Implement security using WSE by enabling WS-Security features to secure your SOAP messages. However, be cautious about compatibility and testing, as issues might arise.

### Steps to Get Started

1. **For WCF**:
   - Create a new WCF service project in Visual Studio (make sure it targets .NET 3.5).
   - Define your service contracts and implement your methods.
   - Configure `web.config` to set up `basicHttpBinding` with the required security settings.
   - Test your service using a WCF client or a simple console application.

2. **For WSE 3.0**:
   - Ensure you have installed WSE 3.0 on your development environment.
   - Navigate to your ASMX service and add the necessary WSE components.
   - Use the WSE 3.0 configuration tool to configure the security settings.
   - Test the service with clients targeting .NET 3.0.

### Conclusion
For a project with a long-term perspective, I recommend going with WCF in .NET 3.5, as it provides more modern security features and flexibility. In contrast, while WSE can work, it's less scalable and more prone to issues as technology evolves. Ultimately, your decision might also depend on the specific security needs and compatibility considerations of your clients.

### 1. Support for `display: none;` in Email Clients

The support for `display: none;` and other CSS properties varies significantly across email clients:

- **Web-based clients (e.g., Gmail, Yahoo)**: Most web clients do not support `display: none;`. These clients often strip out or ignore CSS that hides elements, so items marked with `display: none;` may still be rendered (visible) in the email.
  
- **Desktop clients (e.g., Outlook)**: Microsoft Outlook, in particular, has poor support for CSS and may ignore any properties that attempt to hide content. These clients use the Microsoft Word rendering engine, which does not conform well to web standards.

- **Mobile clients (e.g., iOS Mail, Android)**: Mobile clients tend to be slightly better in handling basic CSS, but caution is still advised. Relevant testing is necessary to ensure design integrity.

To summarize, using `display: none;` is generally not recommended due to inconsistent behavior across email clients.

### 2. Viewing Emails in Plain Text Format

If a recipient views an email in plain text format:

- The email client will strip out any HTML or CSS styling.
- This means that any content hidden using CSS (`display: none;`) will be displayed in plain text. There are no guarantees that the email client will convert the HTML to text while retaining hidden elements, so it is best to avoid relying on CSS for hiding content.

### 3. Testing Email Rendering Across Clients

To see how your emails will look across different email clients, consider using the following tools:

- **Litmus**: Provides comprehensive testing across over 90 email clients and devices to see how your emails render. 
- **Email on Acid**: Similar to Litmus, it offers tools for previewing emails in various environments before sending them out.
- **Mailtrap**: Useful for capturing emails in a safe testing environment.

These tools can save you time and effort in troubleshooting rendering issues before your emails reach recipients.

### Additional Tips for Hiding Elements

If you need to hide elements in emails, consider the following approaches, keeping in mind limitations:

- **Fallback Strategies**: As you mentioned, using multiple fallback methods can help. For example:
  ```css
  font-size: 0;
  max-height: 0px;
  overflow: hidden;
  opacity: 0;
  visibility: hidden;
  display: none;
  mso-hide: all; /* For Outlook */
  ```

  ```html
  <!--[if !mso]><!-->

  </style>
  <!--<![endif]-->
  ```

Crafting HTML emails requires an understanding of the capabilities and limitations of various email clients. Using inline styles instead of block or external styles is essential, relying on tables for layout instead of divs, and carefully considering how to hide content is crucial to maintaining consistent rendering across clients. Tests across different platforms are vital before any email is sent out.

To address your questions regarding the support for JSON documents in Amazon DynamoDB, let's break them down:

### 1) How can I use this if I am making a request directly to the service? Do I just set the M value to the entire JSON object?

Yes, when you're making a request to DynamoDB and want to store a JSON document, you can directly represent the JSON object as a map in your request. In DynamoDB terms, the JSON object is mapped to a DynamoDB data structure as follows:

- The top-level JSON object corresponds to a DynamoDB `Map` (represented with the `M` type).
- JSON key-value pairs become attributes in the DynamoDB item.
  
For example, if your JSON looks like this:

```json
{
  "UserId": "123",
  "Name": "John Doe",
  "Attributes": {
    "Age": 30,
    "Occupation": "Engineer"
  }
}
```

You would send this to DynamoDB using a `PutItem` request with a representation like this:

```json
{
  "TableName": "YourTableName",
  "Item": {
    "UserId": { "S": "123" }, // String
    "Name": { "S": "John Doe" }, // String
    "Attributes": { // Map
      "M": {
        "Age": { "N": "30" }, // Number
        "Occupation": { "S": "Engineer" } // String
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The keys in your JSON correspond to the attribute names, and the values are represented in their corresponding DynamoDB data types (S for String, N for Number, M for Map, etc.).

### 2) Can indexes be included in the JSON document? Will DynamoDB be able to figure this out?

Indexes in DynamoDB are defined at the table level and cannot be included directly within the JSON document itself. When you define a DynamoDB table, you specify the primary key (which can be a Hash key or a combination of a Hash and a Range key) as well as any secondary indexes. 

DynamoDB needs predefined schema for the key(s) and index(es) so it knows how to store and retrieve your data efficiently. So, you must ensure that you design your items, including the keys, in accordance with the indexes you have created.

For example, if you have a primary key like `UserId` and you want to create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) on the `Occupation` attribute, you must have these fields defined and structure your JSON accordingly when you insert documents. 

When performing operations, ensure that the attributes needed for indexing are included in the JSON objects you submit to DynamoDB, but they are not part of the JSON document's structure for indexing purposes.

### Summary

- For inserting JSON documents, represent them as Maps in your DynamoDB requests.
- Indexes must be defined at the table level and cannot be included in the JSON document itself.
- Ensure your JSON includes the fields necessary for any indexes you’ve set up when making requests to DynamoDB.

If you plan to efficiently manage and structure your data storage in DynamoDB, following these patterns will help you make the most of its capabilities, particularly as they relate to JSON document support.

title: How to run 10 long-running functions repeatedly at specific times, avoiding overlapping execution?
ground_truth_answer:
Here is a CronosTimer class similar in shape with the System.Timers.Timer class, that fires the Elapsed event on dates and times specified with a Cron expression. The event is fired in a non-overlapping manner. The CronosTimer has a dependency on the Cronos library by Sergey Odinokov. This library is a TimeSpan calculator, not a scheduler. Caveat: in its current version (0.9.0), the Cronos library is capped to the year 2499. This limit exists to avoid looping through 9999 year for unreachable Cron expressions.

using Cronos;

/// <summary>
/// Generates non-overlapping events according to a Cron expression.
/// </summary>
public class CronosTimer : IAsyncDisposable
{
    private readonly System.Threading.Timer _timer; // Used also as the locker.
    private readonly CronExpression _cronExpression;
    private readonly CancellationTokenSource _cts;
    private Func<CancellationToken, Task> _handler;
    private Task _activeTask;
    private bool _disposed;
    private static readonly TimeSpan _minDelay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500);

    public CronosTimer(string expression, CronFormat format = CronFormat.Standard)
    {
        _cronExpression = CronExpression.Parse(expression, format);
        _cts = new();
        _timer = new(async _ =>
        {
            Task task;
            lock (_timer)
            {
                if (_disposed) return;
                if (_activeTask is not null) return;
                if (_handler is null) return;
                Func<CancellationToken, Task> handler = _handler;
                CancellationToken token = _cts.Token;
                _activeTask = task = Task.Run(() => handler(token));
            }
            try { await task.ConfigureAwait(false); }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (_cts.IsCancellationRequested) { }
            finally
            {
                lock (_timer)
                {
                    Debug.Assert(ReferenceEquals(_activeTask, task));
                    _activeTask = null;
                    if (!_disposed && _handler is not null) ScheduleTimer();
                }
            }
        });
    }

    private void ScheduleTimer()
    {
        Debug.Assert(Monitor.IsEntered(_timer));
        Debug.Assert(!_disposed);
        Debug.Assert(_handler is not null);
        DateTime utcNow = DateTime.UtcNow;
        DateTime? utcNext = _cronExpression.GetNextOccurrence(utcNow + _minDelay);
        if (utcNext is null)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Unreachable date.");
        TimeSpan delay = utcNext.Value - utcNow;
        Debug.Assert(delay > _minDelay);
        _timer.Change(delay, Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan);
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Occurs when the next occurrence of the Cron expression has been reached,
    /// provided that the previous asynchronous operation has completed.
    /// The CancellationToken argument is canceled when the timer is disposed.
    /// </summary>
    public event Func<CancellationToken, Task> Elapsed
    {
        add
        {
            if (value is null) return;
            lock (_timer)
            {
                if (_disposed) return;
                if (_handler is not null) throw new InvalidOperationException(
                    "More than one handlers are not supported.");
                _handler = value;
                if (_activeTask is null) ScheduleTimer();
            }
        }
        remove
        {
            if (value is null) return;
            lock (_timer)
            {
                if (_disposed) return;
                if (!ReferenceEquals(_handler, value)) return;
                _handler = null;
                _timer.Change(Timeout.Infinite, Timeout.Infinite);
            }
        }
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Returns a ValueTask that completes when all work associated with the timer
    /// has ceased.
    /// </summary>
    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        Task task;
        lock (_timer)
        {
            if (_disposed) return;
            _disposed = true;
            _handler = null;
            task = _activeTask;
        }
        await _timer.DisposeAsync().ConfigureAwait(false);
        _cts.Cancel();
        if (task is not null)
            try { await task.ConfigureAwait(false); } catch { }
        _cts.Dispose();
    }
}

Usage example:

CronosTimer timer = new("30 6,14,22 * * MON-FRI");
timer.Elapsed += async _ =>
{
    try
    {
        await LongRunningAsync();
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex);
    }
};

In this example the LongRunningAsync function will run at 6:30, 14:30 and 22:30 of every working day of the week.

You can find detailed documentation about the format of the Cron expressions here.

For simplicity, the Elapsed event supports only one handler at a time. Subscribing twice with += without unsubscribing with -= results in an exception.

When working with a Silverlight application that needs to communicate with a Django backend using Piston for REST APIs, you're correct that Silverlight has limitations regarding the use of certain HTTP verbs such as PUT and DELETE. Silverlight primarily supports GET and POST methods. To work around this issue, you can employ several strategies:

### 1. Use POST for PUT and DELETE

You can use POST requests to carry out the actions intended for PUT and DELETE. This can be achieved by including the desired action (e.g., `PUT` to update or `DELETE` to remove) in the body of the POST request. On the server side, you would need to modify the Django Piston handler to check the body of incoming POST requests for specific actions and handle them accordingly.

**Example Implementation:**

- **Client-Side (Silverlight):**
  You would send a POST request and include a parameter indicating the intended operation.

  ```csharp
  var request = (HttpWebRequest)WebRequest.Create(apiUrl);
  request.Method = "POST";
  request.ContentType = "application/json";

  var data = new {
      action = "PUT", // or "DELETE"
      resourceId = id, // ID of the resource you want to modify/delete
      updatedData = newData // data to update if action is PUT
  };

  using (var streamWriter = new StreamWriter(request.GetRequestStream()))
  {
      string json = JsonConvert.SerializeObject(data);
      streamWriter.Write(json);
      streamWriter.Flush();
  }
  ```

- **Server-Side (Django/Piston):**
  You would check for the action in the POST request body:

  ```python
  from piston.handler import BaseHandler
  from piston.utils import rc

  class ResourceHandler(BaseHandler):
      model = MyModel
      # ... other configurations

      def create(self, request):
          data = request.DATA
          action = data.get('action')

          if action == 'PUT':
              # Handle the update logic
              resource_id = data.get('resourceId')
              # Logic to update the resource with resource_id
              return rc.CREATED  # or rc.SUCCESS if the operation was successful

          elif action == 'DELETE':
              # Handle the delete logic
              resource_id = data.get('resourceId')
              # Logic to delete the resource with resource_id
              return rc.DELETED  # or rc.SUCCESS if the operation was successful

          return rc.BAD_REQUEST  # For unsupported actions
  ```

### 2. Create Custom URLs

Another way to accommodate the Silverlight limitation is to create custom URLs for DELETE and PUT operations that use an intermediary POST request. 

For instance, you could define URLs like `/resource/1/delete` for dealing with deletes or `/resource/1/update` for updates. These routes would accept POST requests and perform the action based on the URL.

### 3. Use JSONP

If you are facing issues with cross-domain requests, consider using JSONP (JSON with Padding) as a workaround for enabling cross-domain requests. However, JSONP won't work with DELETE; it's generally limited for GET requests.

### 4. Client-Side Proxies

If possible, you could implement a proxy that sits between the Silverlight client and the Django server, converting requests to the appropriate HTTP method.

### Conclusion

The most straightforward and commonly used approach in your scenario is probably to reformulate the POST request to include the desired action as described. This allows you to keep using Piston without needing to heavily customize it or run into the limitations imposed by Silverlight. Always ensure to handle security aspects such as CSRF tokens and validate input to maintain the integrity of your application.

### 1. Understanding the Requirement
You want to use the high-level `Estimator` API while also leveraging the low-level threading mechanisms (specifically the `Coordinator`) to read input data in an efficient, distributed manner. This often involves a strategy to manage data ingestion in a way that can effectively feed multiple GPUs.

### 2. Using Input Functions

It's crucial to ensure that tensor feeding works seamlessly for your model. Since using queues directly with `tf.train.QueueRunner` and `tf.train.Coordinator` is less common with the `tf.data` API, you can still achieve your goals through a custom pipeline.

### 3. Define Your Input Function
Here's a rough structure of how your input function could look:

```python
import tensorflow as tf

def input_fn(batch_size):
    # Load and preprocess data
    dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((features, labels))

    # Shuffle, repeat, and batch the dataset
    dataset = dataset.shuffle(buffer_size=10000)
    dataset = dataset.batch(batch_size)
    dataset = dataset.prefetch(buffer_size=tf.data.experimental.AUTOTUNE)

    return dataset
```

### 4. Custom Estimator

```python
estimator = tf.estimator.Estimator(model_fn=my_model_fn)

```

While `tf.data.Dataset` handles many threading issues for you, if you still want to use a `Coordinator`, you can create threads for custom data loading while the estimator is training. However, it's advised to let the `tf.data` API take care of threading since it is optimized for this purpose.

```python
threads = []

# Start the enqueue threads
for _ in range(num_threads):

    t.start()
    threads.append(t)

# Ensure that on termination, all threads are joined properly
coord.join(threads)
```

```python
        estimator.train(input_fn=lambda: input_fn(batch_size))
finally:

```

To solve the problem of removing the trailing text "Metro Filer:" from your input while preserving the key part ("Jack: Grow up far away. He loves food Hotdogs, Hamburgers, and steak. It has a lot more text."), you can utilize `awk` with a field separator. The following `awk` command can help achieve this:

```sh
echo "$new" | awk -F ': ' '{print $1 ": " $2}'
```

### Explanation

1. **`echo "$new"`**: This outputs the value of the variable `new`.

2. **`awk -F ': '`**: This tells `awk` to use ": " (colon followed by a space) as the field separator. This means that `awk` will split the line into fields based on this separator.

3. **`{print $1 ": " $2}`**: In the print statement:
   - `$1` refers to the first field, which is "Jack".
   - `": "` is added to reconstruct the section of the string that has the key.
   - `$2` refers to the second field, which contains the rest of the sentence after removing "Metro Filer:".

### Complete Example

Here’s how you can run the command in a script or directly in the terminal:

```sh
new="Jack: Grow up far away. He loves food Hotdogs, Hamburgers, and steak. It has a lot more text. Metro Filer:"
echo "$new" | awk -F ': ' '{print $1 ": " $2}'
```

### Handling Other Variables

As you mentioned you have 100+ other variables, you can iterate over them similarly in a loop or by applying the command to a list of variables.

```sh
for var in "${variables[@]}"; do
    echo "$var" | awk -F ': ' '{print $1 ": " $2}'
done
```

You can support different screen sizes by using ConstraintLayout:

ConstraintLayout allows you to create large and complex layouts with a flat view hierarchy (no nested view groups). It's similar to RelativeLayout in that all views are laid out according to relationships between sibling views and the parent layout, but it's more flexible than RelativeLayout and easier to use with Android Studio's Layout Editor.

You can use those attributes to specify your views size in precents:

app:layout_constraintWidth_percent=".5"
app:layout_constraintHeight_percent=".5"

For example, single button that is equal to 50% of the screen both in height and width:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout 
  xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
  xmlns:app="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res-auto"
  xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
  android:layout_width="match_parent"
  android:layout_height="match_parent">


<Button

    android:layout_height="0dp"

    app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
